turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Jack asked if it would be sufficient to provide a reference from Lady Bloxham, in order to verify his claim about the house in Belgrave Square.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell expressed her incredulity at the audacity of Mr. Worthing's claim to own a house in Belgrave Square, remarking that a respectable family such as her own would never be so careless as to forget the exact number of their residence.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell told Mr. Worthing that a house in Belgrave Square was a significant expense, and one would expect a gentleman of his supposed standing to be able to provide more substantial evidence of his claims.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell asked Mr. Worthing if he could provide the names of any respectable families who would vouch for his character and standing in society.

turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: Gwendolen insisted that she knew perfectly well who she was engaged to and that it was none other than the real Jack Worthing, not some imposter trying to deceive her mother.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Jack explained that he had indeed been in a bit of a hurry when he made the claim about the house in Belgrave Square, but he had been assured by his solicitor that the property was indeed his, and he had not had time to produce the necessary documents.

turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: Gwendolen told her mother that she was fed up with these absurd questions and that she knew perfectly well what she was doing, and that her marriage to Jack was not something to be questioned or doubted.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell declared that she would not consider a man who could not provide a suitable explanation for his family's background and social standing to be a suitable husband for her daughter.

turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: Gwendolen exclaimed that she was not going to stand for this inquisition much longer and that she would not be swayed by her mother's disapproval.

turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: Gwendolen stood up and declared that she would have a word with her mother, and that she expected her mother to treat Jack with the respect due to him.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Jack told Lady Bracknell that he understood her concerns, but he wished to assure her that he had never intended to deceive anyone about his family's background, and that he hoped she would consider his sincerity.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Jack explained that he had been adopted by a family of good standing, and that his adoptive parents had done their best to provide for him and give him a respectable upbringing.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Jack explained that, although he had never known his biological parents, his adoptive family had always been open and honest with him about his adoption, and that he had never felt any need to hide this information.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell told Jack that his explanation was satisfactory, but that she still required further information about his adoptive family before she could consider him a suitable match for her daughter.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Jack asked if there was any further information his adoptive family could provide to alleviate Lady Bracknell's concerns, and if there was anything specific that she needed to know.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell asked Jack if his adoptive parents were still living, and if he could provide any evidence of their social standing and reputation in the community.

turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: Gwendolen demanded to be let down from the carriage, insisting that she would not be left out of the conversation any longer.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell told Gwendolen that she would let her down from the carriage presently, but that she must first see that Jack had provided the necessary information about his adoptive family.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell asked Jack to provide documentation of his adoptive family's social standing, specifically their membership in any respectable clubs or organizations.

turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: Gwendolen asked her mother if she was so concerned about Jack's family that she couldn't even trust him to have a respectable club membership.

opening.speaker: Gwendolen
opening.text: Gwendolen told Lady Bracknell that she was engaged to Mr. Worthing.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell asked Gwendolen and Mr. Worthing to pardon her, as they were not engaged to anyone. She explained that when they did become engaged, she or Mr. Worthing's father, if his health permitted, would inform them of the fact. An engagement should come as a surprise to a young girl, and it was hardly a matter she could arrange for herself. While she was making inquiries, Gwendolen would wait for her below in the carriage.

opening.speaker: Gwendolen
opening.text: Gwendolen called out to Lady Bracknell.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell told Gwendolen to wait for her in the carriage.

opening.speaker: Gwendolen
opening.text: Gwendolen replied to Lady Bracknell that she would wait for her.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell told Mr. Worthing to take a seat.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Jack stood tall, his eyes locked on Lady Bracknell, and said that he preferred to remain standing, rather than take a seat.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell informed Mr. Worthing that he was not on her list of eligible young men, although she had the same list as the Duchess of Bolton. However, she was willing to enter his name if his answers were satisfactory. She asked him if he smoked.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Mr. Worthing admitted to Lady Bracknell that he smoked.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell was pleased to hear that Mr. Worthing smoked. She believed that a man should have an occupation. There were too many idle men in London. She asked Mr. Worthing how old he was.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Mr. Worthing told Lady Bracknell that he was twenty-nine.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell thought that twenty-nine was a good age to get married. She believed that a man who wanted to get married should know either everything or nothing. She asked Mr. Worthing which category he fell into.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Mr. Worthing replied to Lady Bracknell that he knew nothing.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell was pleased to hear that Mr. Worthing knew nothing. She believed that ignorance was a delicate and exotic fruit that should not be tampered with. She stated that education was unsound and produced no effect in England. If it did, it would be a danger to the upper classes. She asked Mr. Worthing about his income.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Mr. Worthing told Lady Bracknell that his income was between seven and eight thousand a year.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell asked Mr. Worthing if his income came from land or investments.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Mr. Worthing replied to Lady Bracknell that his income came from investments.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell thought that Mr. Worthing's income was satisfactory. She stated that land was no longer a profit or pleasure, but rather a means of gaining position and losing it. She asked Mr. Worthing about his country house.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Mr. Worthing told Lady Bracknell that he had a country house with some land, but he did not depend on it for his income. In fact, the poachers were the only ones who made anything out of it.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell asked Mr. Worthing how many bedrooms his country house had. She also asked if he had a town house, as a girl like Gwendolen could not be expected to reside in the country.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Mr. Worthing told Lady Bracknell that he owned a house in Belgrave Square, but it was let by the year to Lady Bloxham.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell asked Mr. Worthing who Lady Bloxham was.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Jack observed that Lady Bracknell went out very little, and that she was a lady considerably advanced in years.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell asked Mr. Worthing what number his house in Belgrave Square was.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Mr. Worthing told Lady Bracknell that his house was number 149.
